analysis.one_liner: Blocks the Education Department from writing rules tying college access to federal student aid to job outcomes.
analysis.headline: A lone senator's bill to block the Education Department's gainful employment rules died in committee with zero cosponsors and no hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have forbidden the Secretary of Education from using any federal money to write regulations or guidance about the term "gainful employment" in the Higher Education Act. Schools must show they prepare students for gainful employment to qualify for federal student aid, and the Obama administration was preparing rules to enforce that requirement against colleges whose programs leave graduates unable to earn enough to repay loans. The bill would have stopped that enforcement before it started. [S2][S3]
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, colleges whose programs lead to poor job outcomes would keep unrestricted access to federal student aid dollars without new accountability tests. The for-profit career college sector, the main target of the gainful employment rules, would have gained the most.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits the Secretary of Education from using any federal funds to issue regulations or guidance on the meaning of "gainful employment" in the Higher Education Act, preventing the enforcement rule from being written. [S3]
Would shield the requirement that schools prepare students for gainful employment from any new interpretation the department might adopt. [S2][S3]

analysis.who_pays: Students who borrow federal loans to attend programs that do not lead to gainful employment would keep paying for low-value degrees, and taxpayers would keep backing loans for those programs. The Department of Education would be barred from a rulemaking it had begun.

drawbacks.text: Supporters' objection: a career schools advocate would argue the gainful employment rule was federal overreach that could force legitimate vocational programs to close and reduce access to career education. [S2]

The bill's core effect would be to remove a planned test of whether career and for-profit college programs actually lead to jobs that pay enough to repay student loans, leaving students with the debt and no performance check. [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill has a narrow purpose and a real cost. Stopping a rule through a funding prohibition is blunt, and the rule it would block is the main accountability mechanism over a sector that draws billions in federal student aid while many of its graduates struggle to repay loans. Any benefit to colleges avoiding paperwork would come at the expense of students and taxpayers bearing the risk of bad programs.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate health and education committee on the day it was introduced, never got a hearing, markup, or floor vote, and expired when Congress ended in January 2011. [S5][S1]

narrative.text: Sen. James Risch introduced the bill on September 23, 2010, near the end of the 111th Congress. [S5][S1]
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions. [S5]
No further action appears in the record; the bill died in committee when the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011. [S5][S1]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the Education Department kept its authority to write the gainful employment rules, and the for-profit college sector failed to block them through this bill. Students and taxpayers kept a path to accountability over career programs financed with federal aid.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The Education Department and student borrowers

for.name: Sen. James E. Risch
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it on the Senate floor on September 23, 2010. [S5][S1]

against.name: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.role: Senate HELP Committee chair (Sen. Tom Harkin, D-IA)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup after its referral; it died in committee with no further action in the record. [S5]

against.name: Education Department under President Obama
against.what_they_did: Was preparing gainful employment rules that this bill was written to block; its rulemaking continued after the bill died. [S3][S2]

sides.party_line_note: A single Senate Republican sponsored the bill, it drew no cosponsors from either party, and no committee action followed. [S4][S5]

industries.note: The gainful employment rules this bill would block are aimed mainly at for-profit colleges whose programs draw heavy federal student aid while leaving many graduates with debt they cannot repay. The bill would have entrenched their access to those aid dollars without job-outcome checks. [S2][S3]

These schools also fall under the gainful employment requirement, and legitimate programs would gain relief from paperwork and program closure risk. But students and taxpayers lose the protection that the federal aid they receive is tied to programs that actually lead to work. [S2][S3]
